title: Generative AI for Business | Cohere
gist: A Cohere explainer/marketing post lays out the standard enterprise generative-AI playbook (six use-case categories, key adoption risks, a three-stage adoption process) and argues that as the technology commoditizes, competitive advantage shifts from model access to how well an organization applies its own proprietary data and expertise.

insights.claim: Cohere frames enterprise generative AI use cases as clustering into six categories: knowledge search/retrieval/synthesis (often via RAG), content creation and transformation, conversational assistance, software development, data analysis and decision support, and workflow automation/AI agents.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: This taxonomy is the vendor's own segmentation of the enterprise AI market and can be used as a checklist for benchmarking competing platforms' use-case coverage.
insights.locator: Here are some of the main ways businesses are using the technology

insights.claim: Cohere describes retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a two-step process: a retrieval system first finds information relevant to the user's query, then the generative model uses that retrieved information as context to produce its answer.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A concise, vendor-stated definition of RAG mechanics, useful as a baseline to evaluate whether a given product's 'RAG' claim matches this standard architecture.
insights.locator: This often works through retrieval-augmented generation

insights.claim: Cohere distinguishes AI agents from standard workflow automation by autonomy: agents determine what to do next dynamically based on the task, available tools/information, and results of earlier actions, rather than following a predefined fixed sequence of steps.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: This adaptive-vs-scripted distinction is the operative definition investors should use to separate genuine 'agentic' product claims from rebranded rules-based automation.
insights.locator: AI agents offer more adaptive automation

insights.claim: Cohere argues the main barrier to enterprise AI value is not technology capability but business/technical viability — production deployments require reliable data, integration with existing systems, and infrastructure meeting scale and performance needs, and organizations that adopt AI without a clear business case risk added cost and complexity without commensurate value.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A vendor explicitly warning against ROI-less adoption is a useful counter-signal to hype-driven enterprise AI spend, and a data/integration-readiness gap remains the practical bottleneck to watch for enterprise AI vendors' deployment timelines.
insights.locator: There is no shortage of possible business uses

insights.claim: As AI systems gain broader access to sensitive data and permission to act within other business applications, security, privacy, and operational risk rises correspondingly, requiring organizations to define access limits, determine when human review is needed, and assign clear accountability for AI-driven outcomes.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Governance/access-control tooling scales in importance with agent autonomy, pointing to a growing enterprise AI-governance software need adjacent to the core model layer.
insights.locator: Security, privacy, and operational risks can increase

insights.claim: Cohere lays out a three-stage enterprise adoption path: (1) define business objectives and assess data/systems/governance/workforce readiness, (2) select a solution approach — packaged applications, configurable AI platforms, or direct foundation-model builds, deployed provider-hosted, private cloud, or on-premises — and (3) operationalize the solution and continuously monitor quality, usage, cost, and business impact post-deployment.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: This buy-vs-build-vs-platform and hosting-location framework mirrors how enterprise buyers are actually evaluating AI vendors, relevant for assessing which deployment model (packaged app, platform, or foundation model access) captures the most enterprise spend.
insights.locator: While the path to AI adoption varies

insights.claim: Cohere argues that as generative AI becomes more widely accessible to businesses, the underlying technology itself will become less of a competitive differentiator, with durable advantage instead coming from how effectively an organization uses AI to streamline operations and turn its own unique data and expertise into better decisions, products, and services.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: This is a model-commoditization thesis from a foundation-model vendor itself: it implies value capture in enterprise AI shifts toward proprietary-data application layers and away from raw model access, worth weighing against Cohere's own positioning as a model provider.
insights.quote: The more durable advantage will come from how effectively organizations use it to streamline operations and turn their unique data and expertise into better decisions, products, and services.
insights.locator: As generative AI becomes more widely accessible

insights.claim: Cohere points to its own coding assistant, described as 'North Mini Code,' as the company's first model built specifically for developers, offered as an example of software-development use cases for generative AI.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A self-referential product mention rather than independent evidence; useful only as confirmation that Cohere is expanding into developer-focused coding models alongside its enterprise-search/RAG positioning.
insights.locator: Further reading: Introducing North Mini Code
